name: Midac

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Midac was an Irish hero. He was the son of Colga of the Hard Weapons, a warrior from the land of the Danes. Colga invaded Ireland because it was the one seagirt island not under his control. The Fianna defeated his men, and Oscar slew Colga himself. Midac, a boy, survived the battle. Fionn mac Cumhaill chose not to kill the boy. He brought Midac to Almu and raised him as an Irishman. Midac could not forget the death of his father, so he quietly plotted revenge. Fionn's men found the boy sullen and distant, and they persuaded Fionn to send him away. Fionn gave Midac lands in the counties of Limerick and Clare, together with cattle and servants. For 14 years Midac lived in peace near the Shannon. Then the Fianna came to hunt on the fairy hill of Knockfierna near his land. Midac, dressed as a Danish warrior, challenged Fionn with riddling poems. Fionn solved the riddles but did not see who the man was. The band then knew Midac, and he invited them to a banquet in his palace. The palace stood among magic rowan trees, but it was silent and empty. Midac entered, looked at them, and left without a word. Then Fionn saw the trap: a glamour held them hostage in a crude shack. One by one the Fianna fought free, and Diarmait at last cut off Midac's head. A curse still held Fionn until the blood of three foreign kings touched the soil. Diarmait slew the three kings and dragged their heads into the palace. As their blood struck the floor, the palace again became a rude shack. The tale of a trap in a bewitched palace is a common one in folklore.
objective: Document Midac and his bewitched-palace trap for the Fianna.
